commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Ui class to handle all user interaction
commitResults.messageBody:
The main class mixed three concerns: reading input, deciding what each
command means, and printing replies. This first step pulls out the
printing and reading.

Ui now owns the Scanner, the separator line, the banner, the display
date format, and every message the chatbot prints. LebronJames calls
methods such as ui.showTaskAdded(...) instead of System.out.println,
so the wording and layout of a reply can be changed in one place.

Two helper methods moved as a consequence:
- printTaskInstructions and printTaskAdded became Ui methods, since
  they were pure output.
- printTasksOn was split: LebronJames.findTasksOn selects the matching
  tasks (logic) and Ui.showTasksOn prints them (presentation).

Behaviour is unchanged; output was diffed against the previous build
over a script covering every command and error case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskList class to own the list of tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
The main class held a raw ArrayList<Task> and manipulated it directly,
so knowledge of the list was spread across every command branch.

TaskList now wraps that ArrayList and offers only the operations the
chatbot actually needs: add, remove, get, size, and findTasksOn. It
wraps rather than extends ArrayList so the rest of the program cannot
reorder or otherwise disturb a list the save file expects in order.

Range checking moved into TaskList.get, which is the object that knows
how long the list is. LebronJames.parseTaskIndex therefore shrank into
parseTaskNumber: it only checks that a whole number was typed, and the
"Task N does not exist" message now lives in one place instead of being
reached through a taskCount argument passed down from the caller.
findTasksOn moved across for the same reason - it is a question about
the list, so the list answers it.

Behaviour is unchanged; output was diffed against the previous build
over a script covering every command and error case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Turn LebronJames into an object with a run method
commitResults.messageBody:
Everything happened inside a single static main method, so ui, storage,
and tasks were local variables that any future helper method would have
to receive as parameters.

The constructor now creates the Ui and Storage, prints the greeting, and
loads the saved tasks; run() holds the command loop; main() is just
"new LebronJames(DATA_FOLDER, DATA_FILE).run()". This is the structure
the next increment needs: once the loop body becomes Command objects,
those objects are handed the same three fields.

The save-file path is now a constructor parameter rather than something
main reads from a constant, so a test or a second instance could point
the chatbot at a different file.

Behaviour is unchanged; output was diffed against the previous build
over a script covering every command and error case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract Parser and a Command class hierarchy
commitResults.messageBody:
The run loop was still one long if-else chain: each branch worked out
what the user meant, did the work, printed the reply, and remembered
whether to save. Adding a command meant editing that chain, and the
whole thing had to be read to find any single command.

Two classes now share that work:

Parser does all the string handling - finding the command word,
splitting a deadline at /by, rejecting the reserved '|' character, and
checking that a task number is a whole number - and returns a Command
describing what the user asked for. Its methods are static because
parsing depends only on its input.

Command is an abstract class with one execute(tasks, ui, storage)
method, and one subclass per kind of instruction: AddCommand,
DeleteCommand, MarkCommand, ListCommand, OnCommand, ExitCommand. Each
subclass carries out its own job, so run() shrank to reading a line,
parsing it, and executing whatever comes back. Adding a command is now
a new subclass plus one line in Parser, with nothing else touched.

Two design choices worth noting:
- One AddCommand covers to-dos, deadlines, and events. By the time the
  command is built, Parser has already made the right Task, so three
  separate classes would have identical bodies.
- MarkCommand takes an isDone flag rather than being split into
  MarkCommand and UnmarkCommand, for the same reason.
- isExit() replaces the special case that compared the input against
  "bye" inside the loop; the loop now asks the command itself.

Behaviour is unchanged. Output was diffed against master over a script
covering every command and error case, and again over a run that starts
from an existing save file containing a corrupted line.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Make the code more OOP by extracting Ui, Storage (already present),
TaskList, Parser, and a Command class hierarchy, so that each class
has a single responsibility and the main class only wires them
together.

commitResults.messageTitle: Move all classes into a lebronjames package
commitResults.messageBody:
Every class sat in the default (unnamed) package. That works for a
handful of files, but the default package cannot be imported from a
named one, so nothing outside it could ever use these classes, and any
class name added later - Parser, Storage - risked clashing with a
library type of the same name.

All 18 classes now declare "package lebronjames;" and live in
src/main/java/lebronjames/. src/main/java stays the source root, since
later tools look for Java sources there by default; src, main, and java
are deliberately NOT packages.

The classes were moved with "git mv" rather than delete-and-add so git
records them as renames and their history is preserved. The entry point
is now lebronjames.LebronJames, so the run instruction in README.md was
updated to point at its new path.

Behaviour is unchanged; output was diffed against the previous build
over a script covering every command and error case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Split lebronjames into task, command, ui, storage, and parser packages
commitResults.messageBody:
One package of 18 classes gives no hint of how they relate. Splitting
them along the responsibilities extracted in A-MoreOOP makes the design
visible from the folder tree alone:

  lebronjames          LebronJames, LebronJamesException
  lebronjames.task     Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskDateTime, TaskList
  lebronjames.command  Command and its six subclasses
  lebronjames.parser   Parser
  lebronjames.storage  Storage
  lebronjames.ui       Ui

TaskList sits in .task rather than in the root package because it is a
collection of tasks, and grouping it with Task keeps everything that
knows what a task is in one place.

LebronJamesException stays in the root package: every other package
throws or catches it, so putting it in any one of them would make that
package a dependency of all the others.

Classes are now visible across package boundaries only through their
public members, which is what makes the boundaries meaningful. Nothing
had to be widened to make this compile - the one package-private detail,
Task.getDoneFlag, is used only by Todo, Deadline, and Event, which are
in .task with it.

Four javadoc {@link} tags pointed at classes in other packages. They
were written as fully qualified links with a display label, rather than
adding an import used only by a comment - and in the case of
command -> parser, an import that would have made the two packages
depend on each other in both directions.

Behaviour is unchanged. Output was diffed against master over a script
covering every command and error case, and over a run starting from an
existing save file with a corrupted line; javadoc now resolves every
{@link} tag.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Organize the classes into Java packages under src/main/java: a
lebronjames root package holding the entry point and the exception,
with lebronjames.task, .command, .parser, .storage, and .ui grouping
the classes extracted in A-MoreOOP by responsibility.

Brings in the Gradle build files provided with the course template:
build.gradle, the Gradle wrapper (gradlew, gradlew.bat, and
gradle/wrapper/), and the .gitignore entries for Gradle's output.

The branch is not in origin - a fork only copies the default branch -
so it was fetched from nus-cs2103-AY2526S1/ip, the repo this fork was
made from. Both histories share the commit 173d5b3, so this is an
ordinary merge rather than one of unrelated histories.

One conflict: the gradle branch modifies text-ui-test/runtest.sh, but
that folder was deleted upstream in befbd32 ("This primitive test
technique is less useful as AI tools can do similar testing"). The
deletion was kept, so text-ui-test does not come back.

build.gradle still names the template's main class and JAR; adapting it
to this project is the next commit.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Adapt the Gradle build to this project and to Java 25
commitResults.messageBody:
The build files merged from the template were written for the original
Duke project on Java 17, and did not work here:

- application.mainClass was "seedu.duke.Duke". It now points at
  lebronjames.LebronJames, so "gradlew run" starts our chatbot.
- shadowJar produced duke.jar; it now produces lebronjames.jar.
- The Gradle wrapper was pinned to 7.6.2, which cannot run on a Java 25
  JDK at all - it failed with "Unsupported class file major version 69"
  before even reading build.gradle. Upgraded to 9.7.1 by editing
  distributionUrl and then re-running "gradlew wrapper", which also
  regenerates gradlew, gradlew.bat, and gradle-wrapper.jar.
- com.github.johnrengelman.shadow 7.1.2 is unmaintained and cannot run
  on Gradle 8+ ("Could not get unknown property 'convention'"). Replaced
  with its successor, com.gradleup.shadow 9.6.1.

Two additions of our own:

- A Java toolchain pinned to 25, so the build compiles against Java 25
  regardless of which JDK is first on the PATH, and Gradle fetches a
  matching JDK on a machine that lacks one. Without it the build quietly
  follows whatever java the shell happens to have.
- The plain "jar" task is disabled. It produced a second, thinner
  build/libs/ip.jar alongside the fat JAR, which is not a file we ever
  want to hand out; shadowJar's output is now the only artifact.

README.md gained a short table of the Gradle commands.

Verified: "gradlew build" succeeds, "gradlew run" accepts piped input,
and build/libs/lebronjames.jar run standalone with "java -jar" produces
output byte-identical to master over a script covering every command and
error case.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Automate the project build with Gradle: merge the template's
add-gradle-support branch from upstream, then adapt build.gradle to this
project (main class, JAR name, Java 25 toolchain) and upgrade the Gradle
wrapper and shadow plugin to versions that run on Java 25.

The chatbot can now be built and run with 'gradlew build' and
'gradlew run'.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add JUnit tests for TaskDateTime and TaskList
commitResults.messageBody:
Two test classes covering the two methods most likely to hide a bug:
TaskDateTime.parse, which has to decide which of four formats the user
typed, and TaskList's number-to-index conversion, where an off-by-one
would mark or delete the wrong task.

TaskDateTimeTest (13 tests) covers each accepted format, single-digit
days, surrounding whitespace, midnight (which must not be mistaken for
"no time given" and silently dropped when saving), the exact wording of
the error message, and a round trip proving anything written to the save
file can be read back unchanged.

TaskListTest (15 tests) covers both ends of the valid task-number range,
numbers just outside it, the empty list, that a rejected delete leaves
the list untouched, that a to-do never matches a date, and that a
multi-day event is found on its first, middle, and last day.

Two things had to change to make this work:

The tests found a real bug. DateTimeFormatter resolves leniently by
default, so "deadline pay rent /by 2019-02-30" was quietly accepted and
stored as 28 February, and "2019-02-29" in a non-leap year did the same.
The formatters now use ResolverStyle.STRICT, which needs the year
pattern uuuu instead of yyyy, and the chatbot reports the bad date
instead of guessing at one.

The template's JUnit setup did not run on Gradle 9: the test task failed
with "Failed to load JUnit Platform" because junit-platform-launcher is
no longer added implicitly. Declared it explicitly, and moved from the
separate 5.10.0 api/engine pair to the junit-jupiter aggregate at 5.14.4.

All 28 tests pass with "gradlew test". The app's own output is unchanged
apart from the impossible-date fix, checked by diffing a run of the
shaded JAR against master over a script covering every command.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Parser is where a mistake shows up fastest: it decides what the user
meant, so a wrong split leaves "/by" inside a description, and a wrong
prefix check turns "todolist" into a to-do.

ParserTest (29 tests) covers every command word and every way each one
can be malformed - a deadline with no /by, /by glued to the description,
an empty description or date, an event whose /to comes before its /from,
a task number that is missing or not a whole number, a date that does
not exist, the reserved '|' character, blank input, and an unknown word.
It also checks the cases most likely to be got wrong by accident: that
"list all" and "byebye" are not accepted as sloppy spellings, and that
"mark 2" ticks the second task rather than the first or third.

An AddCommand keeps its task privately, so rather than adding a getter
purely for the tests, these execute the command against a real TaskList
and inspect what was added. Storage is pointed at a JUnit @TempDir so no
test touches the real save file.

Task-number range is deliberately tested as a two-step: Parser accepts
"delete 99" because whether task 99 exists is the task list's business,
and the failure is asserted on execute instead.

57 tests pass with "gradlew test".

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add tests for Storage, the task types, and Ui; measure coverage
commitResults.messageBody:
StorageTest (14 tests) covers the save-file contract in both
directions: a missing file is a normal first run rather than an error, a
damaged line costs only that line, every malformed shape is rejected
(too few fields, unknown type, bad done flag, empty description, missing
or unparseable date), a save-then-load round trip returns the same
tasks, dates typed as 2/12/2019 are stored as 2019-12-02, saving an
empty list truly empties the file rather than leaving the old contents,
and the data folder is created on a machine where the app never ran.

TodoTest, DeadlineTest, and EventTest (23 tests) cover the display and
save formats of each task type and their isOn logic, including that a
to-do never matches a date, that a deadline's time of day does not
change which day it falls on, and that an event matches its first,
middle, and last day but not the days either side.

UiTest (11 tests) covers the two places Ui actually decides something -
staying silent when nothing was loaded, and "nothing scheduled" versus a
list of tasks - plus the numbering of the list, since those numbers are
what the user types back into mark and delete. Ui prints to System.out,
so each test swaps in a stream it can read and restores the real one
afterwards.

Also added the jacoco plugin (0.8.15, the first release that reads Java
25 class files) so coverage is a number we can check rather than a
guess. "gradlew test" now writes build/reports/jacoco/test/html.

105 tests pass. Coverage is 85% of instructions and 96% of branches:
task 100%, parser 99%, storage 92%, ui 74%, command 72%. The one low
figure is the LebronJames class itself, which is the interactive run
loop and is covered by running the app instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the JUnit coverage target in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md described how to write code but said nothing about tests, so a
future session would have no reason to keep them up to date.

Added a Testing section recording where tests live, the naming
convention, how to run them, the ~50% highest-value-method coverage
target, and where to find the JaCoCo report that makes the figure
checkable. It also states that tests must be updated in the same change
as the code they cover, and that a failing test means deciding whether
the test or the code is wrong rather than deleting the assertion.

CLAUDE.md already includes AGENTS.md, so this reaches both tools.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Add JUnit tests covering the parsing, task-list, save-file, task-type,
and Ui-decision logic (105 tests, 85% instruction and 96% branch
coverage), fix an impossible-date bug the tests uncovered, repair the
JUnit setup for Gradle 9, add JaCoCo coverage reporting, and record the
coverage target in AGENTS.md.

commitResults.messageTitle: Pin UTF-8 for input and output so the JAR behaves off this machine
commitResults.messageBody:
Testing the shaded JAR the way it will actually be distributed - copied
into an empty folder and run with java -jar - exposed two bugs that only
appear once the app leaves a UTF-8 console.

Storage already fixes the save file's character set as UTF-8, but
Scanner(System.in) and System.out both follow whatever the platform
reports. On a console using, say, windows-1252:

- the basketball in every reply arrived as "?";
- worse, typing "todo café run" wrote "cafÃ© run" into the save file,
  because the input was decoded as windows-1252 and then re-encoded as
  UTF-8 on the way to disk. That corruption is permanent.

Ui's Scanner now states UTF-8 explicitly, matching Storage. main
replaces System.out once with a UTF-8 PrintStream; doing it there rather
than inside Ui keeps Ui free of character-set details and lets UiTest go
on capturing output with System.setOut in the usual way.

Added a Storage test that round-trips an accented description and an
emoji, so this cannot quietly break again.

Verified by running the JAR from an empty folder whose name contains a
space and a bracket - the awkward case the requirements call out - under
a simulated windows-1252 console. 106 tests pass, and the app's output
is otherwise unchanged against master.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how to create, locate, and run the JAR
commitResults.messageBody:
README.md had a table of Gradle commands but did not explain the JAR
itself. Added a section covering the three things someone needs: that
"gradlew shadowJar" creates it, that it lands in build/libs, and the
exact steps to run it - copy into an empty folder, open a command window
there, and run java -jar "lebronjames.jar", with a note on why the
quotes matter for paths containing spaces or brackets.

Also records that the JAR is deliberately not committed and is
distributed through a GitHub release, and where the save file appears
relative to the JAR.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Package the app as an executable fat JAR via the shadowJar plugin,
fix the character-encoding bugs that surfaced when running the JAR
off a UTF-8 console, and document how to create, locate, and run it.

An audit of every public and protected member found the code already
documented apart from one gap: main had no header comment. Added one.

Added package-info.java for all six packages. Per-class Javadoc explains
what each class does but never says what a package is for or why a class
sits in one package rather than another, which is exactly the question
someone reading the folder tree asks first. Each file records the
package's job and the reasoning behind the placements that are not
obvious, such as why LebronJamesException stays in the root package.

Javadoc now reports no missing comments. The five remaining warnings are
all "use of default constructor", raised for classes that declare no
constructor at all; writing empty constructors purely to attach a
comment to them would make the code worse, not better.

106 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Enforce the se-education Java coding standard with Checkstyle
commitResults.messageBody:
The standard was something to remember rather than something the build
checked, so compliance would drift as soon as attention moved on.

Added the checkstyle plugin wired to config/checkstyle/checkstyle.xml,
which is se-education's own configuration for the intermediate Java
coding standard. It runs as part of "gradlew build", so a violation
fails the build instead of surviving to review.

It found 33 violations, all genuine:

- 15 import-order errors. Project imports were mixed into the java.*
  group; they now form their own group, and every import block is sorted
  within its group.
- 17 indentation errors, all in the switch in Storage.parseTask, whose
  case labels sat at the same level as the switch itself.
- 8 declaration-order errors in TaskDateTime. The strictFormat helper
  had been written between two blocks of static fields, and the public
  ACCEPTED_FORMATS constant came after private ones. The method moved
  down to the other methods and the constant up above the private
  fields.
- 2 line-wrapping errors in ParserTest, where a wrapped argument began
  with an opening parenthesis that belongs at the end of the line above.

Recorded the standard in AGENTS.md, along with the Git commit message
conventions from se-education, so future changes follow both.

Checkstyle now reports no violations, and 106 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commitResults.messageTitle: Add find command to search tasks by keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
Once a list grows past a screenful, "list" stops being a useful way to
locate a task, and the only alternative was reading through everything.

"find book" now shows every task whose description contains the keyword.
The search ignores capitalisation, so "book" finds "Read Book", and it
matches inside words, so "book" also finds "bookshop" - the more
forgiving behaviour for someone half-remembering what they typed. A
keyword may contain spaces, so "find read book" searches for the phrase.

The work is split along the boundaries the earlier increments
established: TaskList.findTasksWithKeyword answers the question about
the list, Ui.showMatchingTasks prints the result, Parser recognises the
new word, and FindCommand joins the two. Nothing in the run loop
changed.

Also added the command to the start-up instructions, since that text is
what tells a new user what the chatbot can do.

12 new tests cover matching, capitalisation, partial words, multi-word
keywords, every task type, an empty list, a missing keyword, and that
"finder" is not treated as a find. 118 tests pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Complete the Javadoc coverage: document main, and add package-info.java
for all six packages recording what each package is for.
